Samuels c. Ville de Gatineau

2025 QCCS 429

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

THE HONOURABLE

_____________________________________________________________________

RAYMOND SAMUELS

Plaintiff

v.

VILLE DE GATINEAU

and

MATHIEU BRAZEAU

and

GUILLAUME CHOQUETTE-BUSSIÈRE

and

JONATHAN DESJARDINS

and

NICOLAS GAGNON

and

SHAWN MAHAR

(

OVERVIEW

[
1
]

The Plaintiff seeks my recusation by way of an
application titled
Motion to Recuse Judge
(
Motion to Recuse
).

[
2
]

Subsequent to the hearing on 12 December 2024 in
relation to various interlocutory applications, which proceeded normally and
without any issue being raised about apprehension of bias, the Plaintiff launched
a stream of emails to the Court starting on 23 December 2024, including a PDF
of his
Motion to Recuse.
In the latter, he calls into question my
impartiality within the meaning of article 201 paragraph 2 of the
Code of
Civil Procedure
(
CCP
).

[
3
]

At the hearing on 12 December 2024, I was seized
of the following three interlocutory applications:

3.1.

the
Plaintiff’s
Motion for state-supported counsel and a stay of execution
against the Quebec Human Rights Tribunal
(Plaintiff’s
Motion for a
Lawyer
);
[1]

3.2.

the
Plaintiff’s
Application for a jurisdictional trial transfer from the Quebec
Human Rights Tribunal to the Quebec Superior Court
(Plaintiff”s
Application
for Transfer
);
[2]

and

3.3.

the
Defendants’
Avis de dénonciation des défendeurs de moyens préliminaires
déclinatoires de compétence et en irrecevabilité de la demande introductive

(Defendants’
Application to Dismiss
),
[3]
which seeks to dismiss the
Plaintiff’s originating application at the Superior Court titled
Application
for leave to appeal a judgment rendered in the course of a proceeding
(
Application
to Appeal
).

[
4
]

The underlying proceedings are at the Human
Rights Tribunal,
[4]

where the Plaintiff is suing the Defendants for damages in connection with
alleged incidents in 2018 and 2019 involving police officers of the City of
Gatineau.

[
5
]

In the initial claim at the Human Rights
Tribunal filed by the Commission des droits de la
personne et des droits de la jeunesse on behalf of the Plaintiff, it is alleged that he is the victim of discriminatory profiling
based on the intersection of race, colour, and sex. In that claim, he is identified
as a 6 foot 1 inch tall, anglophone Black man with dreadlocks residing in the
Ottawa area.
[5]

The Commission subsequently withdrew from the case and the Plaintiff has
continued it.

[
6
]

The matter is at the Superior Court because of
the Plaintiff’s
Application to Appeal,
which he filed as an originating
application because he seeks the Court’s intervention against a scheduling decision
of a judge of the Human Rights Tribunal.

[
7
]

I remain seized of the three applications described
above because the conclusion of the hearing on 12 December 2024 was to set down
a deadline of 14 January 2025 for the Plaintiff to submit his response to two
cases cited by the Defendants and to send his version of the chronology of
proceedings. The same deadline applies for the Defendants to communicate their
version of the chronology of proceedings.

[
8
]

On 23 December 2024, 12:24 p.m., the Plaintiff
sent an email to various officers of the Court and the Defendants’ lawyer,
notifying them of his intention to seek my recusation. This email was followed
up by another one at 3:39 p.m., attaching his unsigned
Motion to Recuse,
[6]
with a
Notice of Presentation
for hearing on 9 January 2025.

[
9
]

The Plaintiff sent various other emails on:

•

24 December 2024 at 10:27 a.m.;

•

31 December 2024 at 11:37 a.m.;

•

2 January 2025 at 7:25 p.m.;

•

3 January 2025 at 10:37 a.m.;

•

3 January 2025 at 11:05 a.m.

[
10
]

On 6 January 2025, the coordinating judge for
the district of Gatineau, Justice Jean Faullem, wrote to the parties informing
them that, in accordance with article 205 CCP, I will be the judge presiding
over the
Motion to Recuse
on 9 January 2025, the date of presentation
chosen by the Plaintiff.

[
11
]

Later on 6 January 2025, Associate Chief Justice
Jean-François Michaud wrote to the Plaintiff to confirm that my colleague
Justice Carole Therrien, who had dealt with previous applications in the file,
is not seized of this matter and that the
Motion to Recuse
is
presentable before me pursuant to article 205 CCP. The Plaintiff has been
insisting since the hearing on 12 December 2024 that Justice Therrien should be
the judge hearing all of the applications in this case.

[
12
]

The stream of emails from the Plaintiff
continued after these two letters from my colleagues, but I will not list them
here, for the sake of brevity.

[
13
]

In response to the
Motion to Recuse
, the
Defendants filed an application to dismiss under article 51 CCP titled
Demande
en rejet de la demande en récusation de l’honorable juge Azimuddin Hussain,
J.C.S.
dated 30 December 2024 (
Demande en rejet
).

[
14
]

For the reasons set out below, I dismiss the
Motion
to Recuse
, with costs, and I dismiss the
Demande en rejet
without
adjudicating it on the merits, and without costs.

ANALYSIS

1.

Applicable principles

[
15
]

On the matter of judicial impartiality, the law
establishes a strong presumption of impartiality that is not easily displaced.
[7]

[
16
]

Therefore, the Plaintiff has a heavy burden of
satisfying the test for a reasonable apprehension of bias by showing that there
is a “real likelihood or probability of bias”.
[8]

[
17
]

The test for a reasonable apprehension of bias has
been formulated in the caselaw of the Supreme Court of Canada as follows:

the apprehension of bias must be a reasonable one, held by reasonable
and right minded persons, applying themselves to the question and obtaining
thereon the required information.
[…] that test is
what
would an informed person, viewing the matter realistically and practically—and
having thought the matter through—conclude. Would he think that it is more
likely than not that
[the
decision-maker], whether consciously or unconsciously, would not decide fairly.
[9]

2.

Application of above principles
to the present case

[
18
]

The Plaintiff presents a litany of grounds
seeking to justify my recusation.

[
19
]

The Defendants make the following
characterizations of those grounds:

19.1.

“accusations de la plus haute gravité,
lesquelles sont assénées sans modération”;
[10]

19.2.

“Aucune personne raisonnable ne pourrait en
arriver à de telles conclusions”;
[11]

19.3.

“élucubrations saugrenues”;
[12]

19.4.

“état d’esprit déraisonnable, non-ancré dans le
réel”;
[13]

19.5.

“motifs frivoles et dilatoires”;
[14]

19.6.

“représentations répétées, calomnieuses et
diffamatoires”;
[15]

19.7.

“attitude contestataire, frondeuse et
belliqueuse”.
[16]

[
20
]

The following are the Plaintiff’s various
grounds invoked in support of his
Motion to Recuse
, in his own words:

20.1.

“Circumstantial evidence of collusion between
the trial judge and opposing Counsel consistent with a Deep State operation
unknown to the Quebec Superior Court”;
[17]

20.2.

“Bigotry”
[18]

/ “Antisemitism”
[19]

/ “Muslim-related religious extremist political ideology”;
[20]

20.3.

“Conspiracy to deny of legal representation in
contravention of the
Quebec Charter
in order to facilitate an improper /
unlawful motion by opposing Counsel”
[21]

and “Judge attempting to perpetrate extra-legal authority which exceeds his
statutory powers—
Ultra vires
”;
[22]

20.4.

“Obstructing the Plaintiff’s access to files”;
[23]

20.5.

“Obstructing the court interpreter hired by the
plaintiff”.
[24]

[
21
]

All of these grounds are without foundation, to
say the least. I address them below, tracking the above numbered list. That
being said, the very act of repeating the baseless accusations and then
responding to them gives them more credit than they deserve.

2.1

Ground 1

[
22
]

There is no collusion between the Court and the
lawyer for the Defendants, and there certainly is no such thing as a “Deep
State operation” here, whatever that means.

[
23
]

The Plaintiff seeks to find something nefarious
in the fact that there seems to have been a misunderstanding about the correct
courtroom at the start of the hearing on 12 December 2024, which both parties
attended remotely by Teams. The Plaintiff apparently logged in to room 11 but
the hearing was in room 3.

[
24
]

Such misunderstandings happen in the normal
course of things, and the reasonable, informed person would know that this is
not the basis for a conclusion on the issue of bias.

[
25
]

The Plaintiff also alleges that Justice Therrien
“was improperly displaced by the prevailing trial judge in order to
specifically perpetrate a Deep State operation against the Plaintiff which is
consistent with the experiences of the plaintiff in Ontario”.
[25]

[
26
]

Litigants cannot choose the judges they want to
preside over their cases. An order of special case management under article 157
CCP is required before it can be said that a specific judge has been assigned
to a case to deal with all of the proceedings in relation to that case.

[
27
]

No such order exists in the present case, and
therefore judges are assigned to it according to availability of judges and the
prerogatives of the coordinating judge administering the practice roll for the
day of hearing. Again, the reasonable, informed person would know this and
would not see in this any kernel for a finding of bias.

[
28
]

At the hearing of the
Motion to Recuse
,
the Plaintiff tried to make much of article 48 CCP as a basis for what are
actually two distinct arguments, although this was not always clear from the
submissions. The
Motion to Recuse
itself makes no mention of this
provision.

[
29
]

First, the Plaintiff seems to be arguing that,
because I was appointed for the district of Montreal, I somehow
“inappropriately presided” over the hearing on 12 December 2024 in the district
of Gatineau, and that, absent an order of the Chief Justice of the Superior
Court, Justice Therrien must continue in the file since she previously dealt
with some interlocutory matters in the file.

[
30
]

Second, the Plaintiff seems to be arguing that
article 48 CCP serves as basis for his
Application for Transfer
. In
other words, according to him, the provision allows for the transfer of his
file from the Human Rights Tribunal to the Superior Court.

[
31
]

Article 48 CCP reads as follows:

At any stage of a proceeding, the chief
justice or chief judge may, by way of exception, order, even on their own
initiative, that a case, a trial or an application relating to the execution
of a judgment be transferred to another district in the interests of the
parties or of the third persons concerned or if warranted on serious grounds.

À toute étape d’une instance, le juge en
chef peut exceptionnellement, dans l’intérêt des parties ou des tiers
concernés ou encore si d’autres motifs sérieux le commandent, ordonner, même
d’office, le transfert du dossier, de l’instruction ou d’une demande relative
à l’exécution du jugement dans un autre district.

[
32
]

Regarding the first argument made by the
Plaintiff, on a plain reading of the provision, article 48 CCP is inapplicable
since it applies only to scenarios where the transfer of a case from one
district to another is contemplated. It does not speak to, still less prohibit,
the movement of judges from one district to another.

[
33
]

Regarding the second argument, the Court will
address this in its judgment on the
Application for Transfer.

[
34
]

In any event, a reasonable, informed person
would read article 48 CCP and would know that it is irrelevant for the analysis
on the issue of bias.

2.2

Ground 2

[
35
]

As for the Plaintiff’s cocktail of accusations
of bigotry, antisemitism, and “Muslim-related religious extremist political
ideology”, this comes after the hearing of 12 December 2024. At the hearing
itself, no such issue was raised.

[
36
]

Given the contrived and counterfactual nature of
these accusations, the appearance of the accusations in the
Motion to Recuse

is both shocking and perplexing, as is the Plaintiff’s use of the n-word, in
addition to references to lynching and “racist cabal”, in his emails sent to
the Court.
[26]

[
37
]

The Plaintiff disclosed his Jewish identity by
informing the Court towards the end of the hearing on 12 December 2024 that his
celebration of Hanukkah had to be taken into account when setting the deadline
for the next round of filings. He asked for a period of four weeks counting
from the hearing, and specified 14 January 2025 as his preferred deadline. I
granted his requested deadline, without any hesitation.
[27]

[
38
]

I note from the Plaintiff’s Exhibit 4 attached
to his
Motion to Recuse
that he embarked on an internet search and cites
in his arguments the blog of someone who had negative comments about my
interventions as a lawyer in a highly publicized constitutional trial that took
place in 2020.

[
39
]

Citing other people’s opinions from the vast,
multifarious, and cacophonous universe of the internet and social media is no
basis to allege reasonable apprehension of bias against a judge. The judicial
system would grind to a halt with such an approach.

[
40
]

A reasonable, informed person viewing the matter
realistically and practically, and having thought the matter through, would
find no grounds for questioning my impartiality in connection with the
Plaintiff as a Black and Jewish person. In general, conclusory allegations, which
by their nature do not rely on any actual facts, do not meet the test for
reasonable apprehension of bias.

[
41
]

The Plaintiff’s accusations are wholly unfounded
and gratuitous. They are aimed at intimidating, and exacting the greatest
amount of reputational harm. The Plaintiff is surely aware that social norms
dictate that such allegations are not to be made lightly, and thus when they
are made, they are not without a deleterious impact.

2.3

Ground 3

[
42
]

The Plaintiff alleges that there is a “[c]onspiracy to deny legal representation”
[28]

because the “trial judge appears to be colluding with opposing counsel to
document a list of judicial proceedings outside of the Superior Court, which
has involved the Plaintiff which were never declared by these outside courts to
be vexatious in any way”.
[29]

[
43
]

The Plaintiff claims that I am “attempting to
perpetrate extra-legal authority” and that I have concluded that he does not
have a right to a lawyer.

[
44
]

The latter accusation is a curious one since I
have not even made a decision on the Plaintiff’s
Motion for a Lawyer
,
which is one of the applications that I was seized of at the hearing on 12
December 2024.

[
45
]

Moreover, it is false to allege that the
Defendants’ lawyer engaged in an “apparent legal ambush strategy supported by
the judge” in citing two cases rebutting the Plaintiff’s
Motion for a Lawyer
.

[
46
]

It was open to the Defendants to respond orally
to the
Motion for a Lawyer,
[30]
and
there is no ambush where the Plaintiff has been given an opportunity to respond
to the two cases cited by the Defendants. The Plaintiff has been given that
opportunity, with a first deadline of 14 January 2025, and then a new deadline
as set out further below.

[
47
]

This period for the opportunity to respond to
the two cases cited by the Defendants was granted to the Plaintiff without
hesitation by the Court, as explained above.

[
48
]

As for the allegation that the Court is
“colluding with opposing counsel to document a list of judicial proceedings
outside of the Superior Court”, the Plaintiff adds that there is “apparent
prejudicial bias of the judge who appears to be seeking to collude with Crown
Counsel in order to perpetrate an apparent sham proceeding” because the Court
ostensibly asked the Defendants’ lawyer “to provide him with a list of all the
Plaintiff’s judicial review activities outside of the Superior Court”.
[31]

[
49
]

There is no collusion or bias, and the
Plaintiff’s description needs to be corrected.

[
50
]

The Plaintiff seems to be referring to the fact
that, at the hearing of 12 December 2024, I asked both parties to submit a
chronology of proceedings. There is no order requiring them to do so, but I
made it clear at the hearing that I would find it useful to have from both
parties a chronology of relevant proceedings to date.

[
51
]

Among other exchanges on this point during the
hearing, I specified to the Plaintiff towards the end of the hearing that his
own
Application for Transfer
requires an understanding of the whole
context.

[
52
]

It is by having the larger procedural context of
the case that the Court can better understand, for example, the Plaintiff’s
Application
to Appeal,
which the Defendants seek to dismiss on a preliminary basis. The
Court can also then better understand what is entailed by the Plaintiff’s
Application
for Transfer
, namely to have his file at the Human Rights Tribunal
transferred to the Superior Court, should that application be granted.

[
53
]

Far from seeing the exercise in adversarial
terms, the Plaintiff should see it as an opportunity to present to the Court an
analytical tool that would support his pending applications.

[
54
]

In any event, the Plaintiff’s disagreement with
the exercise cannot be converted into a reasonable apprehension of bias. The
reasonable, informed person viewing the matter would not conclude that the
decision-maker would decide unfairly.

2.4

Ground 4

[
55
]

The Plaintiff alleges that the Court engaged in
“obstruction” of his access to files “which the trial judge directed that the
Plaintiff review in relation to his request to transfer his human rights claim
from the Quebec Human Rights Tribunal to the Quebec Superior Court”.
[32]

[
56
]

There is no such obstruction, and again, the
Plaintiff’s description needs to be corrected.

[
57
]

What the Plaintiff seems to be referring to is
the fact that I kept the physical file with me after the hearing on 12 December
2024, since the file is still active and I will eventually have to rule on
three applications.

[
58
]

It is standard practice for judges to keep the
physical file with them when the file is active and they must make decisions in
them. Again, the reasonable, informed person viewing the matter would know
this, and would not conclude that this is the basis for a reasonable
apprehension of bias.

[
59
]

Moreover, the Plaintiff seems to have
misunderstood the Court’s directions. The Court gave the opportunity to the
Plaintiff to review
his own files
and verify if he has an electronic
version of his
Application for Transfer
.

[
60
]

That being said, misunderstandings happen in the
normal course of things, and all that is necessary is to clarify them. They are
not a basis for casting aspersions or making allegations about obstruction.

[
61
]

Since the Defendants’ lawyer provided, at the
hearing on 12 December 2024, what he had in his file, i.e. a PDF document
titled “Notice of Presentation-
Application for Trial Transfer
”, the
Court gave an opportunity to the Plaintiff to send to the Court the electronic
version of his
Application for Transfer
if the version sent by the
Defendants’ lawyer was not the right one.

[
62
]

The minutes of hearing for 12 December 2024 set
this out:

Mtre. Daponte just sent by email a PDF document titled
“Notice of presentation” dated 15 May 2023, which seems to be, according to
him, the electronic version of the application for transfer filed by Mr.
Samuels;

Mr. Samuels can send to the Court the electronic
version of his application for transfer if the version sent by Mtre. Daponte is
not the right one.

[
63
]

The electronic version of the proceeding, mentioned
above, was meant by the Court to come from the Plaintiff’s own files, in the
same way that the lawyer for the Defendants pulled the electronic version of
the
Notice of Presentation
from his own files.

[
64
]

In its disposition below, the Court repeats the
option given to the Plaintiff to send to the Court the electronic version of
his
Application for Transfer
.

[
65
]

The reasonable, informed person viewing the
matter would not conclude that there is anything here that justifies an
accusation of bias.

[
66
]

In any event, if the Plaintiff wants to verify a
proceeding in the physical file, I will return the physical file to the
courthouse in Gatineau upon signing of the present judgment so that the
Plaintiff can consult it as he wishes.

2.5

Ground 5

[
67
]

The Plaintiff alleges that there was
“obstruction” of the interpreter retained by him to translate when the Court
and the lawyer for the Defendants conversed in French.
[33]
He
states, “It was as if the Judge intentionally didn’t want to plaintiff to be
able to understand most of what was being said in order to make it easier for
the trial judge to render verdicts in favour of opposing counsel.”
[34]

[
68
]

The reality is the opposite.

[
69
]

I note the Defendants’ accurate description of
the situation: “Devant le peu de proactivité de cette personne pour effectuer
la traduction, le juge a participé à traduire certains arguments juridiques,
dans le but de sauvegarder les droits de toutes les parties intéressées”.
[35]

[
70
]

Normally, interpreters in the court process
assert themselves and ask hearing participants to stop in order to give time to
the interpreters to translate. It is only the interpreter who knows how much
talking is enough before he or she asks participants to stop, the Court cannot
guess.

[
71
]

In any event, the reasonable, informed person viewing
the matter would not conclude that there is anything here that justifies an
accusation of bias.

2.6

Pattern of conduct

[
72
]

In addition to directly addressing the grounds
invoked by the Plaintiff in connection with his
Motion to Recuse
, I also
note the pattern of conduct of the Plaintiff in seeking the recusation of
judges whom he perceives as being unfavourable to him, whether that perception
has any foundation or not.

[
73
]

The reasonable, informed person, viewing the
matter realistically and practically—and having thought the matter
through—would conclude that the Plaintiff’s pattern of conduct insisting on
recusation of judges serves to undermine the credibility of the present
Motion
to Recuse
. Asking for the recusation of judges seems to be part of the Plaintiff’s

modus operandi
.

[
74
]

The Plaintiff sought the recusation of Justice
Catherine Pilon in the underlying proceedings at the Human Rights Tribunal, her
scheduling decision in relation thereto being the stated basis for the
Application
to Appeal
.

[
75
]

As it happens, Justice Magali Lewis of the Human
Rights Tribunal informed the Plaintiff at a hearing on 16 October 2024 that
Justice Pilon no longer sits at the Tribunal and will therefore not be hearing
the underlying proceedings in any event.
[36]

[
76
]

He also sought the recusation of my colleague
Justice Catherine Mandeville, who was presiding a hearing to set the date to
hear the Plaintiff’s appeal of his conviction in Municipal Court pursuant to

section 452
of the
Highway Safety Code
.
[37]

[
77
]

Justice Mandeville dismissed his application on
11 December 2023, and the Court of Appeal dismissed the Plaintiff’s application
for leave to appeal given the lack of jurisdiction.
[38]

[
78
]

Under the analysis of pattern of conduct, the reasonable,
informed person viewing the matter realistically and practically would also
consider the observation of Justice Sylvia Corthorn of the Ontario Superior
Court of Justice.

[
79
]

Justice Corthorn noted in the context of
litigation between the Plaintiff and his father, leading to a general finding
by her of vexatious conduct on the part of the Plaintiff in Ontario
proceedings, that the Plaintiff subjected two of her colleagues to the highest
level of disrespect when the outcome of litigation was not in his favour:

Regional Senior Justice McNamara and Justice Roger have
been subjected to the highest level of disrespect—questioning their respective
integrity and judicial independence.  That is how Raymond responds when
the outcome of litigation is not in his favour.
[39]

[
80
]

Placed in the context of the Plaintiff’s pattern
of conduct in relation to other judges, which further reinforces the points I made
above in response to the grounds invoked by the Plaintiff, his
Motion to
Recuse
does not have any credibility.

2.7

Conclusion and next steps

[
81
]

In light of the above, the Plaintiff does not
succeed in displacing the strong presumption of judicial impartiality.

[
82
]

As for the Defendants’
Demande en rejet
,
while many of the observations contained within it are accurate and the Court
has cited some of them, the Court will apply its discretion in the particular
circumstances of the present case and dismiss it as being unnecessary to
adjudicate on the merits since the Court is dismissing the Plaintiff’s
Motion
to Recuse.

[
83
]

The dismissal of the
Demande en rejet

will be without costs since the Court dismisses it without adjudicating it on
its merits.

[
84
]

At the hearing on 9 January 2025, the Plaintiff
asked for a new date to replace the deadline of 14 January 2025 for the next
round of filings. Initially, he proposed a deadline of 28 February 2025 and the
Defendants countered with 8 February. The Plaintiff then proposed 14 February.

[
85
]

The Court will set down the date of 17 February
as the new deadline so as to give to the parties a clear month as of the
present judgment to prepare their respective filings.

DISPOSITION

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT:

[
86
]

DISMISSES
the
Plaintiff’s
Motion to Recuse Judge
, with costs;

[
87
]

DISMISSES
the
Defendants’
Demande en rejet de la demande en récusation de l’honorable juge
Azimuddin Hussain, J.C.S.
, without adjudicating the application on its
merits and without costs;

[
88
]

FIXES
the following
schedule:

88.1.

By
17 February 2025
at the latest, the
Plaintiff

88.1.1.

will respond, if he wishes, to the caselaw cited
by the Defendants, namely
2016 QCCS 3049
and
2022 QCCS 1516
;

88.1.2.

may send, if he wishes, his version of the
chronology of proceedings;

88.1.3.

may send, if he wishes, an electronic version of
his
Application for Transfer
;

88.2.

By
17 February 2025
at the latest, the
Defendants will communicate their version of the chronology of proceedings.

__________________________________

AZIMUDDIN HUSSAIN, j.S.C.

Raymond Samuels

Self-represented

Plaintiff

Mtre. Mathieu Daponte

FASKEN MARTINEAU
DUMOULIN, sencrl, srl

Lawyer for the Defendants

Hearing date:

9 January 2025

No. 55 on the
plumitif.

[2]
No. 25, 26, 58 on the
plumitif.

[3]
No. 21, 22 on the
plumitif.

[4]
File no. 550-53-000051-220.

[5]
Mémoire de la demanderesse (5 July 2022) at paras 2-4, filed
before the Human Rights Tribunal by the Commission and
attached to the
Motion for a Lawyer.

[6]
